NSF Grant Proposal Pathways To Cybersecurity Careers Submitted April 2022 The U.S.
Bureau of Labor Statistics predicts the growth in cybersecurity employment demand will be 34% in the near future.
This is projected to cause over 700,000 unfilled cybersecurity jobs in the U.S., costing the U.S. economy billions of dollars.
While there exists this dramatic shortage in the cybersecurity workforce, there is a parallel phenomenon that only 4% of entry level cybersecurity positions currently go to people classified as from low-income backgrounds.
This Track 2 S-STEM project, called Pathways To A Cybersecurity Career (P2CC), will support low-income students to graduate with a Master’s degree in Cybersecurity from the University of Rhode Island (URI), and enter the cybersecurity workforce.
The P2CC project will provide yearly scholarships of 1-3 year durations to at least 42 unique recipients over 6 years, with expected retention and graduation rates being at least 90%.
The scholars will be domestic low-income students with academic ability, talent/potential, and with demonstrated unmet financial need.

They will be recruited by a campaign that targets traditionally under-represented groups in the cybersecurity field including women, rational/ethnic minorities, and differently-abled people.
Selection of scholars will be by a panel that has been trained in potential selection biases when evaluating low-income applicants, using a rubric that is designed for equity.
In addition to providing scholarships, the P2CC project will implement curricular and co-curricular interventions for the scholars that will target cognitive and non-cognitive aspects of low-income students’ experiences and success that focus on academic supports, and on increasing the students’ professional identity through exposure to the cybersecurity workforce and professional skills, professional role modeling, participation in student cohorts, faculty mentoring, and building self efficacy.
Intellectual Merit.
The interventions of the P2CC project will adapt, implement, and study the application to cybersecurity education of evidence-based curricular and co-curricular interventions that have been shown to be effective supporting low-income student recruitment, retention, and success in STEM education.

The P2CC project’s primary intervention uses Fitzgerald’s definition of “professional identity” as: “containing the attributes: skills and functions; knowledge values and ethics; personal identity; group identity in the profession; and the influence of the context of the field”.
It applies to cybersecurity education specific professional identity enhancement techniques that Peters has classified as “high impact” for low-income STEM student success, and that have been demonstrated on similar S-STEM projects in Math, Science, and Computer Science.
The project includes a robust evaluation of its primary objectives: 1) produce at least 42 graduates who enter the cybersecurity workforce, 2) evaluate the effectiveness of the support interventions in supporting the success of low-income cybersecurity students, and 3) disseminate the results to assist degree programs at other institutions in supporting the success of low-income students in their cybersecurity education.
The evaluation uses data sources including pre and post surveys of scholars, exit tickets following specific activities, exit interviews, demographic data, academic assessments, and career placement data.

The evaluation performs formative evaluation of the objectives using a formal Plan-Do-Study-Act continuous improvement process, and summative evaluation to facilitate reporting and academic publication.

Broader Impacts. This project impacts the scholars themselves, all of which will be low-income students, by providing them access to a high-quality graduate education in cybersecurity - something that is unattainable by many due to economic hardship, and the lack of available financial aid at the graduate level. The professional identity and academic enhancement interventions will help ensure the success of these scholars. The broader impact will be on both the U.S. cybersecurity workforce, which lacks numbers and diversity of workers , and on the U.S. economy as a whole. By producing more qualified cybersecurity workers from low-income background, the P2CC project will serve as an initial step in starting to tap a woefully untapped talent pool that will help address a U.S. cybersecurity workforce deficit crisis that is costing billions of dollars in losses to the nation’s economy, and affecting international competitiveness of U.S. companies.

CONSTITUTION, BY-LAWS, AND UNIVERSITY MANUAL COMMITTEEReport #2022-2023-19 - EDITORIALFACULTY SENATE, March 23, 2023 Rationale: Update sections of Chapter 8 to reflect the new policy, approved by Faculty Senate onFebruary 23, 2023, for resolving grades of Incomplete.
Proposed changes: 8.53.10 Grades.

Student grades are defined as follows: A – Superior B – Good C – Fair D – Low grade, passing F – Failure I – Incomplete S – Satisfactory, course taught on S-U basis S* – Satisfactory, course taken by a graduate student under the Pass-Fail grading option U – Unsatisfactory, course taught on S-U basis U* – Unsatisfactory, course taken by a graduate student under the Pass-Fail grading option, not calculated into graduate GPA #13-14-2 P – Passing, course taken under the Pass-Fail option NW – Enrolled – No work submitted NR – Enrolled – No grade reported #06-07–22 NC – Enrolled - Not completed, not calculated in GPA 8.53.11 Grades shall be given quality point values as follows: A = 4.00 points A- = 3.70 points B+ = 3.30 points B = 3.00 points B- = 2.70 points C+ = 2.30 points C = 2.00 points C- = 1.70 points D+ = 1.30 points D = 1.00 points F = 0 points U = 0 points U* = not calculated in GPA #13-14-2 NC = not calculated in GPA 8.53.12 Enrolled – No Work Submitted.
In those instances when a student enrolls in a course through the registration process and (1) never attends the course, or (2) stops attending early in the semester, the instructor may record a grade of NW, no work submitted.

The grade will not affect the student’s attempted or earned credits and will have no effect on a student’s QPA. 8.53.13 Enrolled – No Grade Reported.
Assigned by Enrollment Services when the instructor does not submit grade (see 8.54.12). #06-07–22, #21-22-6 8.53.14 Enrolled – Not Completed.
Assigned by Enrollment Services when the instructor does not submit a Change of Grade report to resolve a grade of Incomplete (see sections 8.53.20-8.53-24).

8.56.10 Changes in Records. No grade (including that of NW) shall be changed after it has been reported to and recorded by the Office of Enrollment Services except in the following circumstances. First, a grade may be changed upon written request by the instructor. Second, following an appeals case an instructor’s department chairperson or immediate administrative supervisor shall act on the advice of the appeals committee ( see 8.26.13 ) and change a grade over the instructor’s objection. Third, in the event that the original instructor can no longer be consulted (e.g., having died or moved to an unknown address), the instructor’s chairperson/supervisor can act in the missing person’s stead and initiate a grade change, including the removal of inappropriate NW grades. This shall only happen, however, if an appeals committee has recommended such action in writing. All grade changes must be authorized by the appropriate dean. Entries to a student’s academic record shall not be changed after two years for the undergraduate student and after three years for the graduate student ( s S ee sections 8.26.10 through 8.26.13 for appeals procedures ) . Grade changes for grades received before graduation will not be permitted after graduation unless the change is based on clerical or procedural errors and the change is received and posted to the student’s record by the last day of classes of the semester following the term in which the student graduates (see 8.56.12). #05-06–31

University of Rhode Island Faculty Senate RESOLUTION: To offer a formal statement of solidarity and support to our fellow colleagues and associated communities in Florida RATIONALE: WHEREAS The Manhattan Institute is now issuing templates for dismantling DEI educational initiatives in every state across the country WHEREAS Florida is at the forefront of a nationwide campaign to silence Black voices and erase the full and accurate history and contemporary experiences of Black people WHEREAS Florida College System presidents issued a collective statement affirming their view that some diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives are harmful to higher education WHEREAS Governor DeSantis has explicitly stated his aim to defund and dismantle DEI initiatives as well as the governing body and administrative leadership of The New College, a public institution WHEREAS Governor DeSantis and the Florida House of Representatives made demands in January for information regarding the funding of programs related to diversity, equity, inclusion, and critical race theory at colleges and universities, now intending to bar funding for these programs across the higher education system WHEREAS under Florida's Stop WOKE Act— which has been temporarily enjoined by a federal court from being enforced in higher education settings— endorsement of theories that criticize systemic racism is forbidden, disparagement of these theories is openly allowed and transgressions can be penalized through revoking millions of dollars in state funding WHEREAS public universities and colleges in Florida must nevertheless administer ideological surveys to all higher ed students, faculty and staff, the results of which may be used to drive budgetary decisions WHEREAS students in Florida are nevertheless permitted to seek permission for recording lectures, which may be used in disciplinary or legal actions against faculty WHEREAS all syllabi and reading lists must nevertheless be posted in publicly accessible locations at least 45 days before the start of classes WHEREAS faculty speech in Florida is nevertheless unconstitutionally compelled in some quarters to expose students to ideas they may find “uncomfortable, unwelcome, disagreeable, or offensive,” through syllabi, reading selection and class discussion WHEREAS Governor DeSantis rejected the AP course in African American History, demanding that The College Board excise specific subject areas from the curriculum WHEREAS The College Board stripped down and altered the AP exam for African American History, followed by a statement of regret for failing to immediately denounce the Florida Department of Education and Governor DeSantis's administration, the latter of which commented that African American Studies “lacks educational value.” WHEREAS Governor DeSantis is considering barring all Advanced Placement Exams in Florida

WHEREAS investigations target trans students and employees by demanding information that could potentially compromise patient privacy and discourage individuals from seeking medically appropriate care WHEREAS Black leaders, alarmed by Governor DeSantis, have begun to protest and prepare for 2024 WHEREAS higher education workers are organizing around the country, through growing unions like the United Faculty of Florida (UFF) and new coalitions like Higher Education Labor United, to defend our freedoms and throw a much-needed lifeline to the sinking discussions about higher education in Florida and elsewhere WHEREAS the United Faculty of Florida are welcoming statements of support for their fellow colleagues and associated communities in Florida WHEREAS it is vital that students, faculty, staff, and administrators outside of Florida band together in this moment of crisis to defend the public good of higher education ____________________________________________________________________________________________________________ THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the Faculty Senate of URI extends this statement of solidarity and support to our fellow colleagues and associated communities in Florida.
